data.title: Poll: would you take part in an amnesty for archaeological finds?
data.excerpt: For about 1 month we have been running a poll asking whether people would take part in an amnesty for archaeological finds. Out of 118 respondents, 39 would bring their finds in for expert study and registration but only if the finds were then returned to them, while 29 would hand them over to a museum with no claim to a reward.
data.metaTitle: Poll on an amnesty for archaeological finds
data.metaDescription: Interim results of our poll asking whether people would take part in a possible amnesty for archaeological finds, and what that would mean in law.

children.text: For about 1 month we have been running a poll here with the question:
"If an amnesty for archaeological finds were declared, would you take part in it?"

Its result so far is admittedly in no way scientifically verifiable and of course not binding on anyone. However, given the absence of scientific research or of official statistics on this subject, and given that our site is read by a community of people who may reasonably be assumed to have archaeological finds put away at home for various reasons, I would not ignore the result so far.
It has in fact turned out that there is a fairly large number of people (specifically, as of today,
out of 118 respondents as many as 39
people) who in the event of an amnesty would bring their finds in for the purpose of expert study and registration, but only if the finds were subsequently returned to them. That is a fairly
of those taking part in the vote, and it is questionable whether it is appropriate for such a high percentage to be ignored.

It is worth considering whether, after a possible success of a finds amnesty (which, if it comes about, I assume will apply only to finds that are handed over), it would not be for the good of the cause if the legislator devised an arrangement under which such finds could also be registered.
This could be done, for example, in such a way that after scientific study such finds would be registered and their original unlawful holders (which is what they are today) would become
(not owners, since the owner of finds is the state) of the find, with the proviso that
they would at the same time have a duty to look after the finds
and to safeguard them against loss or theft. Should they decide to sell the finds,
they could only “sell” them to the state

for a finder's reward.
 
 The question, however, is whether those concerned (the holders of the finds) would have any interest in such a form at all.

As for the number of people who in the event of an amnesty would hand their finds over to a museum with no claim to a reward (29 voters), here I think there is nothing to discuss. If only these 29 people handed over their finds, even that would be a great positive, and of course it must be assumed that there will be many more.

So an amnesty would certainly be beneficial, even in its most limited form. Let us hope that at least in that limited form (the handing over of finds) it will be possible to push it through the legislative process.
It is an interesting subject for discussion, even though I assume that a great many archaeologists will not agree with it ....
